bt67yj-k39494-d1e106.summary: Rubric heading for section 3, announcing the topic: how God is in place, and how in time.

bt67yj-k39494-d1e111.summary: The paragraph reasons that since God is in all things, it follows that God is also in place and in time, albeit in a far different way than created things, and announces that, to understand this, three modes by which a thing is said to be in a place must first be considered.
claims: Because God is in all things, God must also be in place and in time, though not in the manner of creatures.
Understanding this requires distinguishing three modes of being in a place.

bt67yj-k39494-d1e127.summary: The paragraph defines the first mode, 'circumscriptive' presence in place, whereby a thing is enclosed, contained, and circumscribed by a definite spatial extent such that its parts correspond to the parts of the place (greater part to greater space, lesser to lesser); this mode belongs only to bodies and is alien to incorporeal things such as soul, angel, and above all to God's nature. It notes that Scripture and the Fathers (citing 3 Kings 8, 2 Chronicles 6, Acts 17, and a liturgical hymn on the Incarnation, with Augustine and Boethius) accordingly deny that God is circumscriptively contained by place, even though as man Christ was circumscribed by the womb of the Virgin; it further explains that corporeal and locative language applied to God (sitting, standing, moving, dwelling) is metaphorical, accommodated to human ways of conceiving, following Augustine.
claims: Circumscriptive presence in place, where a thing's parts correspond point-for-point to spatial parts, belongs only to bodies and cannot apply to incorporeal beings or to God.
Scripture and the Fathers deny that God is circumscriptively contained by any place.

Locative and corporeal language predicated of God in Scripture is metaphorical, accommodated to human modes of understanding, and signifies God's presence or operation rather than literal spatial containment.

bt67yj-k39494-d1e196.summary: The paragraph defines the second mode, 'definitive' presence in place, whereby a thing, though not circumscribed by place, is somewhere and not elsewhere; this is the mode proper to angels, who are present spiritually wherever they act or move things, being present where they operate (citing Damascene and Ambrose). Because angelic power is finite, an angel cannot naturally operate simultaneously in several places at once, but only in one place at a time, of a size proportioned to the extent of its operation upon a body — an extent that cannot be infinite because the angel's power is not infinite.
claims: Definitive presence means being somewhere without circumscription, such that the thing is not elsewhere.
Angels are present definitively, spiritually, wherever they act or operate.
Because their power is finite, angels cannot naturally be simultaneously present and operative in multiple places, and the extent of their presence is bounded by the extent of their operation.

bt67yj-k39494-d1e242.summary: The paragraph defines the third mode, 'eminent' presence in place, understood in two ways: first, by giving being to place itself and locating or containing it (the way God is said to be in all other things, by giving them being and operation); second, by filling place, not as a body fills it, but by giving being to located things and making them be in a place and fill it. This third mode is, on both counts, the most excellent and the one proper to God's manner of being in place, as Aquinas explains (Summa I, q. 8, a. 2).
claims: Eminent presence in place has two aspects: giving being to place as its locating cause, and filling place by giving being to what is located in it.
Eminent presence is the most excellent mode and the one proper to God.
concepts: God as cause of place and of located things

bt67yj-k39494-d1e273.summary: The paragraph extends the threefold distinction to time: a thing is in time either because it is moved by proper motion measured by time (as corporeal things), or because it undergoes change according to affections, measured by aevum (as incorporeal creatures), or because — being immutable and immense, yet the author of all time and change — it causes all else to be measured, a mode proper to God alone, following Augustine (On Genesis Against the Manichees VIII.26). By the same reasoning, God is rightly said to be outside and above all time and place, as taught by Augustine, Jerome (on Isaiah 40), Gregory (on Ezekiel, homily 17), and the Master.
claims: There is a threefold parallel distinction of ways a thing is 'in time,' corresponding to the threefold distinction of ways a thing is 'in place.'
God is in time as the immutable, immense author and measure of all temporal change, a mode proper to him alone.
God is rightly said to be outside and above all time and place.
concepts: divine immutability and transcendence of time

bt67yj-k39494.summary: Capitulum 3 explains how God is in place and in time by distinguishing three modes of being in place — circumscriptive (proper to bodies), definitive (proper to angels), and eminent (proper to God as the giver of being to place and to located things) — and then extends the same threefold structure to explain how God is in time, concluding that God, as immutable cause and measure of all temporal change, transcends both place and time.
claims: There are three modes of being in a place: circumscriptive, definitive, and eminent, proper respectively to bodies, angels, and God.
A parallel threefold distinction applies to being in time, with God's mode being that of the immutable cause and measure of all time.
God transcends both place and time while being truly, though uniquely, 'in' both.
